vignette:
He is 30, Middle Eastern, divorced, and works as a tax inspector, a job that requires him to move between offices, meet with business owners, and spend long hours reviewing records and driving from one appointment to the next. Before the accident, he describes himself as methodical and calm, the kind of person who liked schedules and knew how to keep his emotions private. He had been married for four years, and by his account, the separation had already left him feeling stretched thin, but he was still managing work, paying bills, and trying to keep his life orderly.

The collision happens on an evening drive home after a long day of inspections. He remembers the weather, the traffic, and the ordinary feeling of being tired and eager to get home. Another vehicle comes fast from the side, and in the next instant there is impact, metal folding, glass breaking, and the violent sensation of being thrown. He says he is certain he is going to die. In the minutes after the crash, time feels distorted; he recalls the smell of airbag dust, the sound of people shouting, and the helpless frustration of being pinned in place while his body refuses to cooperate. He does not remember every detail clearly, but the images he does hold are sharp enough to return without warning.

In the days afterward, he is physically sore and shaken, but what unsettles him most is how often the accident comes back to him. He finds himself replaying the moment of impact while sitting at his desk at work or standing in line for tea. He notices that his body reacts before his mind can catch up: his chest tightens when he hears sudden brakes outside, and he startsle easily at horns or screeching tires. Driving, once routine, becomes an ordeal. He begins taking longer routes that avoid busy intersections, and on difficult days he asks a coworker to drive or invents an excuse to postpone a field visit. He tells himself he is being practical, but he also knows he is afraid.

As the weeks pass, sleep becomes lighter and less refreshing. He falls asleep with the television on because silence leaves too much room for the accident to surface. When he does sleep, he wakes abruptly from dreams of being crushed, trapped, or unable to open the car door. In the morning he feels drained, irritable, and behind before the day even begins. At work, he remains competent, but he has to read certain pages twice and catches himself staring at numbers without absorbing them. He is embarrassed by this because his work depends on precision, and he prides himself on being thorough. More than once he notices himself growing unusually tense during a routine roadside inspection, especially if traffic is close or a vehicle passes too quickly. He grips his pen harder, checks the exit, and tries to keep his breathing steady.

He also begins to pull back from other people. His divorce already made him quieter, but now he is even less likely to accept invitations or answer calls after work. Friends ask how he is doing, and he says, “Fine,” because he does not want to explain that he keeps seeing the crushed frame of his car in his mind. He feels ashamed of how vulnerable he is, especially because he expects himself to be the one who handles things. He notices that he is more easily frustrated with his ex-wife during necessary conversations about logistics, and he catches himself becoming short with coworkers over minor delays. At the same time, he feels oddly distant from his own life, as if he is going through the motions while part of him remains on that road, waiting for the next impact.

He starts paying attention to every sound and movement around him when he is in traffic. He scans other drivers constantly, bracing for someone to cut him off. Even when nothing happens, his body acts as though danger is near. He avoids talking about the crash except in brief, factual terms, and when someone presses him, he changes the subject. Yet the memory continues to intrude in quiet moments, especially at night and during long drives for work. He says the accident has not only changed how he travels, but also how he inhabits the world: less freely, less confidently, and with a persistent sense that safety can disappear in a second.
